content: A stye is a localized inflammation of an oil gland located at the edge of the eyelid, where the eyelashes meet the lid. It manifests as a red, swollen bump resembling a pimple and is often tender, particularly when touched. Symptoms of a stye may include a gritty or scratchy sensation, as though a foreign body is present in the eye. Additional symptoms can include sensitivity to light, excessive tearing, and tenderness of the eyelid. The underlying cause of a stye is bacterial infection, typically from skin bacteria that infiltrate the oil glands in the eyelids. These glands are responsible for lubricating the tear film. Styes are comparable to acne pimples that occur on other parts of the body. It is possible to have multiple styes simultaneously. They generally develop over a few days and may resolve on their own by draining and healing. However, a stye can progress into a chalazion, which occurs when an inflamed oil gland becomes completely blocked. A large chalazion may interfere with vision. Individuals with blepharitis, a chronic inflammation of the eyelid margins, are at a higher risk of developing styes. A stye is typically diagnosed through a physical examination by a healthcare provider. Special diagnostic tests are rarely required. It is important to seek medical attention if you experience any of the following: Vision problems A stye that worsens or does not improve within one to two weeks of self-care A stye that becomes very large or painful The presence of a blister on the eyelid Crusting or scaling of the eyelids Redness of the entire eyelid or the eye itself Extreme sensitivity to light or excessive tearing Recurrence of a stye shortly after successful treatment of a previous one Bleeding from the eyelid bump Treatment for styes and chalazions often involves the application of warm compresses for 10 minutes, four times daily. It is crucial not to squeeze or attempt to drain a stye, as this can worsen the infection. Allow the stye to drain naturally. In cases of recurrent or persistent styes, antibiotic creams may be prescribed. Larger styes may require lancing by a healthcare professional to drain the infection. Other eyelid conditions that may resemble styes include: Xanthelasma: These are raised yellow patches on the eyelids, often associated with aging. While harmless, they may occasionally indicate high cholesterol levels. Papillomas: These are pink or skin-colored bumps that are benign but may grow slowly, potentially affecting vision or causing cosmetic concerns. They can be surgically removed if necessary. Cysts: These are small, fluid-filled sacs that may also impact vision. To prevent styes, it is essential to practice good hygiene, such as thoroughly washing your hands before touching the skin around your eyes. For individuals prone to styes, gently cleaning excess oils from the edges of the eyelids may be beneficial. The prognosis for styes is generally excellent, as they often resolve on their own or with simple treatment. However, complications can occur, including: Recurrence of styes Spread of infection to other eyelash follicles Spread of infection to the surrounding eyelid tissue, leading to eyelid cellulitis
